\chapter{Five Verbs at the Core}
\label{ch:ur-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five everyday Urdu verbs by their shared -nā ending, take that ending off to reach the stem, and say what I do in the present with the participle agreeing for gender and the copula agreeing for person. I can write nūn ghunna and baṛī ye, and read maiṅ, haiṅ, nahīṅ and the copula hai off the page.}

The fifth verb runs the whole machine at once: strip -nā from all five infinitives, hold the doubled nūn that keeps jānnā apart from jānā, and put the stem into maiṅ jāntā/jāntī hūṅ.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[honā]{\ur{ہونا} — “to be,” and the ending every Urdu verb wears}

\label{lesson:UR-C06-hona}



\begin{quote}
You can already close an Urdu sentence with \emph{hūṅ} — “am.” It is still spoken rather than written: its last shape is a nūn with no dot, and that letter arrives in the very next lesson. That small word is a fragment of something larger. Here is the whole verb it was broken off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ہونا}} — \emph{honā} — \textbf{to be}
\end{quote}

Read from the right edge: \textbf{\ur{ہ}} \emph{h}, then \textbf{\ur{و}} carrying \emph{o}, then \textbf{\ur{ن}} \emph{n}, then \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}. Every one of those four shapes has already turned up in a word you have met. There is nothing new to decode here, which is rare, and worth enjoying.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending that names every verb}]
\textbf{honā} ends in \textbf{-\ur{نا}} \emph{-nā}. So does every Urdu verb when you name it. English marks a verb's plain name by putting a word in front — \emph{to be, to go, to come}. Urdu marks it by putting \textbf{-nā} on the end, and never uses a separate word for it.

That ending is also a tool. Strip \textbf{-nā} off and what remains is the \textbf{stem}, the piece everything else in the verb is built on. \textbf{honā} minus \textbf{-nā} leaves \textbf{ho-}. Learn the ending once, and every new verb hands you its own stem for free.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{honā} comes from Sanskrit \emph{bhavati}, “becomes,” built on the root \emph{bhū-}. The middle stage of Indo-Aryan softened that \emph{bh-} to \emph{h-}, so \emph{bhavati} thinned to \emph{hoi} and then to \textbf{honā}.

The root is Indo-European: *\emph{b\textsuperscript{h}uH-}, “grow, become.” English kept it in \textbf{be} and \textbf{been}, and — by way of “the place where one dwells” — in \textbf{build}, \textbf{booth}, and \textbf{bower}. Latin held it as \emph{fuī} “I was” and \emph{futūrus}, which English borrowed as \textbf{future}. Greek held it as \emph{phúsis} “nature,” which English borrowed as \textbf{physics}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{honā} — to be
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{honā} minus \textbf{-nā} leaves the stem \textbf{ho-}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{ہونا}} from the right edge
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{honā} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{bhavati} $\to$ English \textbf{be}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ṭhīk}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ending names an Urdu verb? (\textbf{-nā}.) What is left of \emph{honā} once you take that ending off? (\textbf{Ho-}.) Which English verb grew from the same ancient root? (\textbf{Be}.)

Sources: \href{https://openbooks.lib.msu.edu/urdu/chapter/2-7/}{\emph{Basic Urdu}: Personal Pronouns with “To Be”}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DB\%81\%D9\%88\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7\#Urdu}{Wiktionary: \ur{ہونا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nūn ghunna]{\ur{ں} — nūn with the dot taken off}

\label{lesson:UR-W06-nun-ghunna}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ن}. The deep bowl, a lift, and one dot placed low inside the curve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ں}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{same deep bowl} you drew two chapters ago, swept right to left below the baseline — and then you stop. \textbf{No lift. No dot.}

Every other letter so far was identified by what was \textbf{added} to it: nūn's dot, kāf's slash, the three teeth of sīn. This one is identified by what was \textbf{taken away}, and the taking away is the meaning. Its name is \textbf{\ur{ں}} \emph{nūn ghunna}, and \emph{ghunna} is the Urdu word for a nasal hum.

Here is the difference it makes. A dotted \textbf{\ur{ن}} is a full consonant: your tongue touches the roof of your mouth and you say \textbf{n}. A dotless \textbf{\ur{ں}} asks for no consonant at all. It tells you to send the \textbf{vowel before it} through your nose and then stop. In \emph{maiṅ} the tongue never lands.

Two more facts and the letter is yours:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{ں}} closes a word and appears nowhere else. Inside a word, that same nasal hum is carried by the ordinary dotted \textbf{\ur{ن}}, which therefore does two jobs depending on where it stands — a real \textbf{n} in some words, a hum in others. Only at the end of a word does Urdu bother to spell the difference.
  \item Because it ends the word, \textbf{\ur{ں}} has one shape to learn and no joined faces.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Three words, all of them already in your mouth, none of them readable until now. From the right:

\begin{quote}
\ur{میں}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہیں}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{نہیں}
\end{quote}

\emph{maiṅ} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} — \emph{haiṅ} \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nahīṅ} \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{}

The one to dwell on is \textbf{\ur{نہیں}}. It is the word you learned for saying no, in the very first handful of words this book gave you, and it is four letters you can now name one by one: \textbf{\ur{ن،} \ur{ہ،} \ur{ی،} \ur{ں}} — with a dotted nūn opening it and a dotless one closing it, doing two entirely different jobs in a single short word.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ں} — the deep bowl, and then nothing
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{میں}, then \ur{ہیں}, then \ur{نہیں}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{maiṅ}, letting the vowel hum and keeping your tongue down
  \item \emph{Point to:} at the two nūns in \ur{نہیں} and say what each one does
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{ہیں} — and say why it ends on a hum rather than an n
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Write \textquotedblleft{}no.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{نہیں}}.) Write \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{میں}}.) Does your tongue touch the roof of your mouth at the end of \emph{maiṅ}? (\textbf{No} — the hum goes through the nose.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jānā]{\ur{جانا} — “to go,” and two agreements in one sentence}

\label{lesson:UR-C06-jana}



\begin{quote}
Take the ending off \textbf{honā} and say the stem aloud. The next verb gives that same ending a second workout.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{جانا}} — \emph{jānā} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

From the right edge: \textbf{\ur{ج}} \emph{j}, then \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}, then \textbf{\ur{ن}} \emph{n}, then \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}. The \textbf{\ur{ج}} is the one from \textbf{\ur{جی}} \emph{jī}. Strip the \textbf{-nā} and the stem is \textbf{jā-}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the present tense agrees twice}]
“I go” in Urdu is two words after the pronoun, not one:

\begin{quote}
\emph{maiṅ jātā hūṅ} — \textbf{I go} (man speaking) \emph{maiṅ jātī hūṅ} — \textbf{I go} (woman speaking)
\end{quote}

The frame is printed the way you say it rather than the way it is spelled. The \textbf{t} of \emph{jātā} and the \textbf{ū} of \emph{hūṅ} both ride letters you have not been given yet, and a line you cannot decode is not reading practice.

The first word is the stem \textbf{jā-} plus \textbf{-tā}. It says \emph{going}, and it agrees with the \textbf{gender and number} of the person doing it: \textbf{-tā} for one man, \textbf{-tī} for one woman, \textbf{-te} for more than one man or for a respectful singular. The second word is \textbf{hūṅ}, which you already own, and it agrees with \textbf{person} — who is speaking.

Two agreements, split across two words, in one short clause. English makes one agreement at most, and usually none. Say both Urdu lines and let the difference sit in the ear rather than on paper.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jānā} continues Sanskrit \emph{yāti}, “goes,” from the root \emph{yā-}, “travel.” The change from \emph{y-} to \emph{j-} is not a quirk of this word: initial \emph{y-} regularly hardened to \emph{j-} on the road from Sanskrit into the middle stage of Indo-Aryan that Urdu descends from. Meet the law once and it decodes other words later.

English gives nothing here. The \emph{yā-} root travelled north and west into Lithuanian and Slavic rather than into Germanic, so this is a word where Sanskrit is the whole hook and English cannot help.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jānā} — to go
  \item \emph{Strip:} \textbf{jānā} minus \textbf{-nā} leaves \textbf{jā-}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{maiṅ jātā hūṅ}, then \textbf{maiṅ jātī hūṅ}
  \item \emph{Choose:} the ending that fits you — \textbf{-tā} or \textbf{-tī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which word in \emph{maiṅ jātā hūṅ} carries gender? (\textbf{Jātā} — the one built on the stem.) Which one carries person? (\textbf{Hūṅ}.) And which Sanskrit verb stands behind \emph{jānā}? (\emph{Yā-}, “travel.”)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AC\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7\#Urdu}{Wiktionary: \ur{جانا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ānā]{\ur{آنا} — “to come,” which is “go” pointed back at you}

\label{lesson:UR-C06-ana}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{jānā}, then its stem \textbf{jā-}. The opposite direction is the same verb wearing a prefix.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آنا}} — \emph{ānā} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

From the right edge: \textbf{\ur{آ}}, then \textbf{\ur{ن}} \emph{n}, then \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}. That first shape is \emph{alif madd} — alif wearing a small wave — and it is how Urdu writes a long \emph{ā} at the start of a word. It opens \emph{āp} too, which you will be able to spell out once pe arrives. Strip the \textbf{-nā} and the stem is \textbf{ā-}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ānā} continues Sanskrit \emph{āyāti}, and that word is two pieces: \emph{ā-}, “toward,” plus \emph{yā-}, “go.” So the Urdu verb for \emph{coming} is, underneath, the verb for \emph{going} aimed back at the speaker. “Go toward me” is “come.”

You already have the second piece: \emph{yā-} is the same root that hardened into the \textbf{j-} of \textbf{jānā}. One Sanskrit verb, two Urdu words, and the difference between them is a direction marker.

English does the identical trick with a Latin verb: \emph{venīre} “to come” plus a prefix gives \textbf{advent}, \textbf{convene}, \textbf{intervene}, \textbf{prevent}, and \textbf{revenue}. Urdu welds its prefix on the front and lets the seam disappear; English keeps the seam visible.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ānā} — to come
  \item \emph{Pair:} \textbf{jānā} away, \textbf{ānā} toward
  \item \emph{Split:} \emph{ā-} “toward” + \emph{yā-} “go”
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{آنا}}, starting from \emph{alif madd}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{khudā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two pieces are hiding inside \emph{ānā}? (\emph{Ā-} “toward” and \emph{yā-} “go.”) Which Urdu verb shares the second piece? (\textbf{Jānā}.) And what does the stem become once \textbf{-nā} comes off? (\textbf{Ā-}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A2\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7\#Urdu}{Wiktionary: \ur{آنا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[baṛī ye]{\ur{ے} — the big ye, and the end of the sentence}

\label{lesson:UR-W06-bari-ye}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ی}, then \ur{ہ}, then \ur{ں}. An S-curve, a loop, a bowl with no dot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ے}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{wide, flat sweep}. Start high on the right, drop through a long shallow curve that goes \textbf{well below the baseline}, and carry it a long way to the left, finishing \textbf{flat} — with no hook, no lift at the tip, and no dots.

Its name is \textbf{\ur{ے}} \emph{baṛī ye}, \textquotedblleft{}big ye,\textquotedblright{} and the letter you already know, \textbf{\ur{ی}}, is \emph{choṭī ye}, \textquotedblleft{}small ye.\textquotedblright{} Two names, one family, and one test that separates them at a glance:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ur{ی}} \emph{choṭī ye} is narrow and \textbf{curls back up} at its tip
  \item \textbf{\ur{ے}} \emph{baṛī ye} is broad and \textbf{runs out flat}
\end{itemize}

There is a second difference, and it is about where each one lives. Small ye turns up anywhere in a word — opening it, in the middle, closing it. Big ye belongs to the \textbf{end of a word} and turns up nowhere else, which means you will never have to work out its middle face. It has none.

Big ye carries a final \textbf{e} or \textbf{ai} sound.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
Two letters, and the smallest word in Urdu that does real work:

\begin{quote}
\ur{ہے}
\end{quote}

From the right: \textbf{\ur{ہ}}, then \textbf{\ur{ے}}. Say it: \textbf{hai} — \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{}

That is the word you have been ending sentences with since you first said your name, four chapters ago. Read it now.

Two more, both already in your ear:

\begin{quote}
\ur{کیسے}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرے}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{کیسے}} \emph{kaise} — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} with small ye in the middle and big ye at the end, so the pair sit in one word and you can see the difference for yourself. \textbf{\ur{میرے}} \emph{mere} — \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{} before a plural, every letter of it now yours.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twelve letters. Now read the first sentence this book ever gave you, whole, with nothing taken on trust:

\begin{quote}
\ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے}
\end{quote}

\emph{merā nām ... hai} — \textquotedblleft{}my name is ...\textquotedblright{}. Every letter in it is one you can form: \textbf{\ur{م،} \ur{ی،} \ur{ر،} \ur{ا}} — \textbf{\ur{ن،} \ur{ا،} \ur{م}} — \textbf{\ur{ہ،} \ur{ے}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ے} — wide, flat, below the line, no hook at the tip
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ہے} — and say \textbf{hai}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کیسے} — and point at the small ye and the big ye in turn
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{میرا} \ur{نام} ... \ur{ہے} — and say it with your own name in the gap
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which ye curls up at the tip? (\textbf{Small ye, \ur{ی}}.) Which runs out flat? (\textbf{Big ye, \ur{ے}}.) Write \textquotedblleft{}is.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{\ur{ہے}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bolnā]{\ur{بولنا} — “to speak,” and the two layers of Urdu}

\label{lesson:UR-C06-bolna}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the opening without looking: \textbf{shukriyā — jī hā̃ — nahī̃}. Air-trace the five shapes of the thank-you word once. Then return to the three verbs whose stems you pulled from the same ending. Here is a fourth, with one new letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{بولنا}} — \emph{bolnā} — \textbf{to speak}
\end{quote}

From the right edge: \textbf{\ur{ب}} \emph{b}, then \textbf{\ur{و}} carrying \emph{o}, then \textbf{\ur{ل}} \emph{l}, then \textbf{\ur{ن}} \emph{n}, then \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}. Strip the \textbf{-nā} and the stem is \textbf{bol-}.

\textbf{\ur{ب}} is new, and it is worth one careful second. Its body is a single low scoop with \textbf{one dot below}. Hold that skeleton in mind: the very next chapter adds \emph{pe}, which is the identical scoop with \textbf{three dots below} — the \emph{p} you already say in \emph{āp}. Same skeleton, different dot count, different consonant. Urdu builds much of its alphabet this way, so counting dots is a real reading skill and not a fussy detail.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: put it in the frame}]
The stem takes the same two-agreement frame as before:

\begin{quote}
\emph{maiṅ boltā hūṅ} — \textbf{I speak} (man speaking) \emph{maiṅ boltī hūṅ} — \textbf{I speak} (woman speaking)
\end{quote}

Nothing new is being learned there. That is the point of a stem: the machine is already built, and each verb just walks into it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bolnā} goes back to Prakrit \emph{bollaï}, “speaks” — and then the trail stops. A link onward to Sanskrit \emph{brūte} “speaks” has been proposed, but it is not settled, so treat it as a maybe rather than a fact.

That plainness is the lesson. Urdu's everyday verbs are inherited Indo-Aryan and often short-rooted like this, while its formal and literary vocabulary was borrowed from Persian and Arabic and tends to be long, elegant, and easy to trace. Beside homely \textbf{bolnā} sits Persian-derived \emph{guftagū}, “conversation,” from Persian \emph{guftan}, “to speak.” Both are fully Urdu. One is the floor of the house; the other is the ornament on it — and the flowing \emph{nastaʿlīq} hand Urdu is traditionally written in belongs to that same Persian inheritance.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{bolnā} — to speak
  \item \emph{Count:} \textbf{\ur{ب}} one dot below — and say what the three-dot version will be
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{maiṅ boltā hūṅ}, then \textbf{maiṅ boltī hūṅ}
  \item \emph{Sort:} \textbf{bolnā} inherited, \textbf{guftagū} borrowed
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many dots does \textbf{\ur{ب}} carry, and where? (One, below.) How far back can \emph{bolnā} be traced with confidence? (To Prakrit \emph{bollaï}, and no further.) Which layer of Urdu does \emph{guftagū} belong to? (The Persian one.)

Sources: \href{https://openbooks.library.northwestern.edu/zerozabar/chapter/the-urdu-alphabet/}{\emph{Zero Zabar}: The Urdu alphabet}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A8\%D9\%88\%D9\%84\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7\#Urdu}{Wiktionary: \ur{بولنا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jānnā]{\ur{جاننا} — “to know,” a word English has been carrying all along}

\label{lesson:UR-C06-janna}



\begin{quote}
Run the four verbs you have — \emph{honā, jānā, ānā, bolnā} — and pull the stem off each one. The fifth is the closest of them to English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{جاننا}} — \emph{jānnā} — \textbf{to know}
\end{quote}

From the right edge: \textbf{\ur{ج}} \emph{j}, \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}, then \textbf{\ur{ن}}, then \textbf{\ur{ن}} a second time, then \textbf{\ur{ا}} long \emph{ā}. Two separate nūns, written out one after the other, and both are pronounced: hold the \emph{n} long, \emph{jān-nā}, the way English does across the seam of \emph{thin·ness}. Strip the final \textbf{-nā} and the stem is \textbf{jān-}.

That doubling is what keeps \textbf{jānnā} “to know” apart from \textbf{jānā} “to go.” One letter, and the whole meaning turns.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jānnā} continues Sanskrit \emph{jānāti}, from the root \emph{jñā-}, “know.” That root is Indo-European *\emph{ǵneh\textsubscript{3}-}, and English is stuffed with it.

Straight down the Germanic line: \textbf{know}, \textbf{knowledge}, \textbf{can} (once “to know how”), \textbf{cunning}, \textbf{ken}, and \textbf{uncouth} — literally “un-known.” Borrowed from Latin \emph{(g)nōscere}: \textbf{notice}, \textbf{note}, \textbf{notion}, \textbf{cognition}, \textbf{recognize}, \textbf{acquaint}, and \textbf{ignore}, which is “not to know.” Borrowed from Greek \emph{gnōsis}: \textbf{diagnosis}, \textbf{prognosis}, and \textbf{agnostic}.

So the Urdu verb is not a stranger. It is a first cousin of the plainest word English has for the same idea, and every one of those borrowings is another place to hang it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jānnā} — to know, holding the long \emph{n}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{jānā} to go, \textbf{jānnā} to know
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{maiṅ jāntā hūṅ}, then \textbf{maiṅ jāntī hūṅ}
  \item \emph{Run through:} all five — \emph{honā, jānā, ānā, bolnā, jānnā} — stripping each stem
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{jānnā} $\leftarrow$ \emph{jñā-} $\to$ English \textbf{know}, \textbf{notice}, \textbf{diagnosis}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hāfiz}, then say \emph{honā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What single written difference separates \emph{jānā} from \emph{jānnā}? (A second \textbf{\ur{ن}}, held long in speech.) Which two words in \emph{maiṅ jāntī hūṅ} agree, and with what? (\textbf{Jāntī} with gender, \textbf{hūṅ} with person.) And which English verb is the same word as \emph{jānnā}? (\textbf{Know}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AC\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86\%D9\%86\%D8\%A7\#Urdu}{Wiktionary: \ur{جاننا}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
